1.stem: [Academic Talk — Plant Domestication] According to the professor, what is one way plant domestication unintentionally occurred?

options.A: By keeping every planting to a single region
options.B: By carrying seeds between distant regions
options.C: By harvesting plants that retained their seeds longer
options.D: By engineering the genes of seeds in modern laboratories

2.stem: [Academic Talk - Cell Biology] Which version of the older story does the evidence leave in place?

options.A: That an engulfing host acquired the bacterium late, after the scaffolding and the nucleus were finished and in working order.
options.B: That the nucleus and the mitochondrion arrived in one and the same event, the virus supplying one and the bacterium the other.
options.C: That the host had the parts of a complex cell but lived off an exchange with its partner rather than eating it.
options.D: That complexity of this kind cannot arise until the energy supply is in place, so the parts must postdate the partnership.

3.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] Why does the speaker say 'this isn't the only change'?

options.A: To signal that migration is one of several effects still to be described.
options.B: To suggest that migration matters less than it first appears.
options.C: To correct a common misunderstanding about where marine species live.
options.D: To introduce evidence that species are moving toward cooler water.

4.stem: [Academic Talk — Film History] Why does the professor mention that audiences 'didn't need to read English' to enjoy a silent picture?

options.A: To argue that silent pictures were harder for immigrant audiences to follow than the sound films that came later.
options.B: To explain why nickelodeons drew working-class and immigrant crowds, helping cinema become a mass medium.
options.C: To explain why Méliès's staged fantasies drew far larger crowds than Lumière's films of ordinary everyday life.
options.D: To show that most of the films shown in American nickelodeons had actually been made in France, not in America.

5.stem: [Academic Talk — Architecture] How does the professor explain why the arch is structurally advantageous?

options.A: It lets an interior be poured from concrete alone, with no stone used anywhere.
options.B: It removes the need for supporting walls, so no columns or piers are required.
options.C: It turns a tension problem into compression, which stone handles well.
options.D: It removes the weight of the roof entirely, so the walls carry no load at all.

6.stem: [Academic Talk — Marine Biology] What is the professor's central point about coral reefs?

options.A: Bleaching is the point at which the coral has already died and cannot recover.
options.B: The coral polyp lives perfectly well on its own once it has built its skeleton.
options.C: The reef's biodiversity rests on a temperature-sensitive partnership between coral and algae.
options.D: Coral reefs cover most of the ocean floor, which is why they shelter a quarter of marine species.

7.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] Why does the professor describe earthquake swarms and bulging ground?

options.A: To show that thick, sticky magma is the variety lowest in silica content.
options.B: To argue that even the largest eruptions strike with no detectable warning at all.
options.C: To explain the warning signs volcanologists use to anticipate eruptions.
options.D: To describe how runny lava flows slowly down the slopes in Hawaii.

8.stem: [Academic Talk — Linguistics] What is the main idea of the lecture?

options.A: Both innate ability and environment are important for language acquisition.
options.B: Children can learn language equally well at any age with enough exposure.
options.C: Language skills depend entirely on genetics, since the ability to learn is innate.
options.D: All children develop language skills at the same rate, whatever input they hear.

9.stem: [Academic Talk — Marine Biology] Why does the professor describe the coral-algae partnership as the reef's 'weak point'?

options.A: Because the algae slowly eat away the calcium carbonate skeleton the polyp builds.
options.B: Because the partnership works only within a narrow temperature range and fails when water warms.
options.C: Because reefs sit on less than one percent of the ocean floor, leaving them nowhere to expand as seas warm.
options.D: Because the polyp and its algae end up competing for the same food supply.

10.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] In the evening example, what is the opportunity cost of choosing to study?

options.A: Sixty dollars, the value of the concert
options.B: Forty dollars, the value of the work shift
options.C: Zero, because studying costs nothing
options.D: One hundred dollars, the shift plus the concert

11.stem: [Academic Talk — Epidemiology] How does the lecturer regard the claim that whatever survives statistical adjustment is the real effect?

options.A: As a sound rule of thumb, provided the list of measured confounders is long enough to cover income, occupation and smoking.
options.B: As a sign that the direction of causation has simply been reversed, with better health leading people to drink more coffee.
options.C: As evidence that observational studies should be abandoned in favour of laboratory experiments, since adjustment cannot be trusted.
options.D: As an understandable but unsafe conclusion, because adjustment is limited by how coarsely the confounders were recorded.

12.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] What is the professor's main point about glaciers?

options.A: Snow turns into dense ice only after the mass has begun to creep downhill.
options.B: Ice ages are triggered by the ridges of debris, called moraines, that glaciers leave.
options.C: Glaciers carve narrow V-shaped valleys that widen as the ice retreats.
options.D: Glaciers form from compressed snow, flow slowly downhill, and reshape the land.

13.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] Why does the professor describe the factory built on company-owned land?

options.A: To show that building factories is usually a poor business decision
options.B: To illustrate that opportunity cost includes implicit costs with no price tag
options.C: To argue that accountants calculate costs more accurately than economists
options.D: To explain how firms can avoid taxes by owning rather than renting land

14.stem: [Academic Talk — Architecture] Why does the professor single out the Pantheon?

options.A: Because it is the oldest surviving Greek temple.
options.B: Because it showcases a huge domed interior free of interior columns.
options.C: Because it was built entirely from carved stone blocks.
options.D: Because it relied on post-and-beam construction rather than arches.

15.stem: [Academic Talk — Linguistics] What pattern does the professor use as an example of a regular sound change?

options.A: Where Latin has a 'p,' English tends to have an 'f.'
options.B: Where German has an 'f,' Latin tends to have a 'b.'
options.C: Where English has a 'p,' Sanskrit tends to have a 't.'
options.D: Where Greek has a 'k,' Latin tends to have a 'g.'

16.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] According to the professor, what is demand-pull inflation?

options.A: The cost of inputs such as oil or wages rising, with firms passing that on to buyers.
options.B: Too much spending chasing too few goods, prompting sellers to raise prices.
options.C: A one-time jump in the price of a single crop, such as tomatoes after a bad harvest.
options.D: A deliberate two-percent target that policymakers aim for.

17.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] According to the experiments the professor cites, how does losing twenty dollars compare with gaining twenty dollars?

options.A: Losing feels about the same as gaining, since the amounts are equal
options.B: Losing feels roughly twice as strong as gaining the same amount
options.C: Gaining feels stronger than losing because gains are more memorable
options.D: The two feel identical only for experienced investors

18.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] What can be inferred about the importance of tracking plate movements?

options.A: It is used mainly to locate mineral resources along the boundaries where plates collide.
options.B: It helps scientists predict geological hazards and plan safer infrastructure.
options.C: It is useful only for explaining how mountain ranges such as the Himalayas were formed.
options.D: It allows scientists to prevent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions at subduction zones.

19.stem: [Academic Talk — Astronomy] What can be inferred about why scientists value studying comet material?

options.A: Comet ice can be mined as a future fuel source.
options.B: Comets reveal the ingredients present when the planets were forming.
options.C: Studying comets helps predict when they will strike Earth.
options.D: Comets are more common than asteroids in the inner solar system.

20.stem: [Academic Talk - Palaeoecology] Africa is described for three sentences with nothing attaching it to what comes before or after. What is the example doing?

options.A: It identifies the continent from which the vanished faunas of the other landmasses had dispersed, making the losses elsewhere a matter of range contraction.
options.B: It holds the glacial swings constant and varies only how long the animals had lived alongside hominins, sparing a version keyed to first encounter.
options.C: It fixes the earliest secure date for hominin presence anywhere on earth, giving a baseline against which the arrival dates on the other continents can be read.
options.D: It supplies a control showing that heavy-bodied mammals withstand hunting so long as the hunters carry stone rather than projectiles of a later design.

21.stem: [Academic Talk — Plate Tectonics] According to the professor, what evidence supports the idea of continental drift?

options.A: The steady spreading rate that every ridge has held over geological time
options.B: The absence of any recorded earthquakes along the Cascadia subduction zone
options.C: Similar fossils and geological formations found on different continents
options.D: New oceanic crust forming where magma rises along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge

22.stem: [Academic Talk — Art History] In a relief print such as a woodcut, which parts of the block create the printed lines?

options.A: The grooves cut into the surface of the block.
options.B: The raised parts that were left uncut.
options.C: The areas wiped clean before the paper is laid down.
options.D: The areas drawn with a greasy crayon.

23.stem: [Academic Talk — Plate Tectonics] What can be inferred about the Cascadia subduction zone?

options.A: A long quiet period there is not evidence that the zone is safe
options.B: It is less dangerous than the Japanese zone because it has been quiet
options.C: It is a divergent boundary, so it forms new crust rather than large quakes
options.D: It produced the 2011 earthquake described earlier in the talk

24.stem: [Academic Talk — Communication] Why does the speaker add that face-to-face interaction 'remains crucial'?

options.A: To argue that social media has had almost no real effect on communication.
options.B: To introduce the topic of the day's talk before giving examples.
options.C: To limit the claim that social media has completely changed how people interact.
options.D: To explain why the speed of communication has increased.

25.stem: [Academic Talk — Linguistics] What is the professor's main point about how children learn language?

options.A: Children actively work out underlying rules, which is why they make systematic errors.
options.B: Children cannot produce past-tense forms until an adult corrects them.
options.C: Children simply copy the sentences adults say, which is where forms like 'goed' come from.
options.D: Children work out irregular verbs only once grammar is taught in school.

26.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] Why does the professor say most central banks are kept independent from the elected government?

options.A: So that the tool used to bring inflation down cannot also be blamed for unemployment
options.B: So the central bank can raise its key rate whenever unemployment rises
options.C: So politicians cannot use cheap money for short-term gain before an election
options.D: Because the bank's only customers are commercial banks, so the government has no account there

27.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] What can be inferred about why earthquakes are sudden even though plates move slowly?

options.A: Because plates quietly accelerate to many times their usual speed just before a rupture.
options.B: Because seismic waves travel outward far more slowly than the plates themselves move.
options.C: Because locked plates store stress for years until the rock slips all at once.
options.D: Because crust welling up at mid-ocean ridges shoves the plates forward in one sudden push.

28.stem: [Academic Talk — Film History] What is the professor's main point about early cinema?

options.A: The nickelodeon failed as a business because five cents was still more than working-class and immigrant audiences would pay, so cinema never grew past being a novelty.
options.B: Georges Méliès invented cinema by pointing a camera at everyday life, workers leaving a factory and a train arriving, while the Lumière brothers built painted sets and staged trips to the moon.
options.C: Early films were technically identical to the movies we know today and differed only in running time, since the Lumière brothers already used the storytelling methods of later features.
options.D: Early cinema grew from two impulses — recording reality and staging the impossible — and became a mass medium through cheap, accessible theaters.

29.stem: [Academic Talk — History] What does the professor suggest about who built the pyramids?

options.A: They were built by slaves forced to work year-round.
options.B: They were built by the scribes during the flood season.
options.C: They were built by farmers working as seasonal laborers while their fields were flooded.
options.D: They were built by foreign prisoners captured in war.

30.stem: [Academic Talk — Psychology] What does the professor imply is a downside of relying on cues to recall memories?

options.A: Cues can distort recall, contributing to unreliable eyewitness memory.
options.B: Cues are effective only for people whose forgetting comes from actual damage to storage.
options.C: Using a cue erases the original memory trace, so a recalled word cannot be found again.
options.D: Depending on cues prevents new memories from forming, so old parking spots crowd out today's.

31.stem: [Academic Talk — Psychology] What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: How researchers measure the discomfort of dissonance by paying participants to lie about a task.
options.B: Why people revise their beliefs when their behavior conflicts with them.
options.C: How the discomfort of conflicting beliefs forces people to abandon their values altogether.
options.D: Why paying people larger sums of money is the most effective way to change what they believe.

32.stem: [Academic Talk — Linguistics] What is the main point the lecturer makes about writing systems?

options.A: All writing systems started as pictographs and remained unchanged.
options.B: They evolved to meet the specific needs of different societies.
options.C: Writing systems are identical across all cultures.
options.D: Writing was only used for religious purposes in ancient societies.

33.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] What happens at a transform boundary, according to the professor?

options.A: One plate dives beneath the other.
options.B: Plates remain completely stationary.
options.C: Plates grind past each other sideways.
options.D: Plates pull apart and new crust wells up.

34.stem: [Academic Talk — Art History] What is the professor's main point about printmaking techniques?

options.A: In every method the ink sits on the raised surface of the block, as it does in a woodcut.
options.B: Lithography, invented around 1800, replaced woodcut and engraving because carving a plate by hand was slow and costly.
options.C: Different techniques put the ink in different places relative to the surface, which changes how the print looks.
options.D: Woodcut and engraving are really the same relief method under two different names.

35.stem: [Academic Talk — Film History] How did Méliès discover that film could make things appear or vanish?

options.A: Partly by accident, when his camera jammed.
options.B: By reading about the technique in a magic manual.
options.C: By projecting films in a nickelodeon.
options.D: By studying the Lumière brothers' factory films.

36.stem: [Academic Talk — Meteorology] Why does the professor say the bottoms of clouds are often all at the same level on a given day?

options.A: Because dust and salt particles float only at one level.
options.B: Because water vapor condenses at the height where the rising air has cooled enough.
options.C: Because wind pushes all the clouds to the same height.
options.D: Because droplets keep merging until they grow heavy.

37.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] How does the professor distinguish inflation from a single price change?

options.A: A single price change always turns into cost-push inflation once firms pass the higher cost along to buyers.
options.B: A single price change is tracked with a price index that measures a basket of typical goods year over year.
options.C: A single price change reduces the purchasing power of money across the whole economy, only more slowly.
options.D: A single price change, like costlier tomatoes after a bad harvest, is just one relative price moving.

38.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] According to the professor, what is notable about the Arctic tern?

options.A: It never migrates farther than a single region.
options.B: It sees more daylight in a year than almost any other creature.
options.C: Its young cannot survive without following the adults.
options.D: It navigates only by Earth's magnetic field.

39.stem: [Academic Talk — Plate Tectonics] What is the professor’s overall point about plate tectonics?

options.A: Its main value is explaining the earthquake activity along faults such as the San Andreas in California
options.B: It is still only a hypothesis that GPS measurements have yet to confirm
options.C: It is a single framework that both explains and helps anticipate a range of geological events
options.D: Plate movement of a few centimeters a year is too slow to affect anyone today

40.stem: [Academic Talk — Zoology] Why do birds using the sun as a compass need an internal clock?

options.A: Because the sun moves across the sky, so birds must correct for the time of day.
options.B: Because the Earth's magnetic field shifts through the day and the clock corrects it.
options.C: Because the stars rotate around the North Star as the night goes on.
options.D: Because clouds can hide the sun, so the bird falls back on its clock.

41.stem: [Academic Talk — Psychophysics] What is the lecturer's position on the textbook practice of treating the criterion as a nuisance parameter?

options.A: He considers it a statistical error that inflates estimates of sensitivity by folding in the observer’s caution.
options.B: He allows it as a laboratory convenience but denies it where the two kinds of error carry unequal costs.
options.C: He rejects it, holding that sensitivity cannot be estimated separately from the criterion at all.
options.D: He accepts it wherever the two kinds of error carry unequal costs, since the criterion is then measurable.

42.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] What is the main idea of the lecture?

options.A: Human activities have no impact on marine life.
options.B: Coral reefs are unaffected by climate change.
options.C: Marine species are migrating to warmer waters.
options.D: Climate change affects marine biodiversity in multiple ways.

43.stem: [Academic Talk — Classics] What is the professor's main point about Greek myths?

options.A: Myths did real work for the Greeks — explaining nature and modeling how to behave.
options.B: The myths were told purely for entertainment, and taught the Greeks nothing about conduct.
options.C: The Greek gods were imagined as flawless and remote, untouched by ordinary human feeling.
options.D: Greek myths were gathered into one sacred book that an organized priesthood taught from.

44.stem: [Academic Talk — Asymmetric information in labor markets] According to the professor, what is one way employers try to reduce the effects of asymmetric information?

options.A: By using probationary periods or performance-based pay
options.B: By refusing to hire workers without degrees
options.C: By ignoring educational credentials
options.D: By offering the same wage to all applicants

45.stem: [Academic Talk — History] What does the professor suggest about why the Renaissance began in the Italian city-states?

options.A: The city-states were the only places with universities.
options.B: Wealth generated by trade funded artists and libraries there.
options.C: The printing press was invented in the Italian city-states.
options.D: The city-states banned classical texts, forcing new ideas to emerge.

46.stem: [Academic Talk — Classics] How did the Greeks explain the changing seasons, according to the professor?

options.A: Through the hero stories of Heracles and Odysseus, which held up examples of courage and cleverness.
options.B: Through Zeus, the king of the gods, hurling his lightning down at the earth from the sky above them.
options.C: Through the punishment of mortals guilty of hubris, the excessive pride the gods always struck down.
options.D: Through the story of Persephone, carried to the underworld each winter and returning each spring.

47.stem: [Academic Talk — Cognitive Dissonance] What is the main idea of the lecture?

options.A: Cognitive dissonance helps explain why people change their attitudes or rationalize behaviors
options.B: Cognitive dissonance shows up only in consumer decisions, such as buying an expensive car or phone
options.C: Cognitive dissonance is a rare phenomenon confined to unusual laboratory experiments like Festinger's
options.D: Cognitive dissonance arises because people simply lack accurate information about their choices

48.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] What is the professor's main point about earthquakes?

options.A: Earthquakes are scattered at random across the interiors of the plates.
options.B: Earthquakes are mostly set off by eruptions along mid-ocean ridges.
options.C: Most earthquakes happen at plate boundaries, where stress builds and suddenly releases.
options.D: All three kinds of plate boundary push the plates directly toward one another, locking them.

49.stem: [Academic Talk — Ecology] Which organisms does the professor identify as decomposers?

options.A: Mainly plant roots taking up nutrients.
options.B: Only earthworms and beetles.
options.C: Mostly fungi and bacteria, along with larger creatures like earthworms and beetles.
options.D: Chiefly the fallen leaves and tissues themselves.

50.stem: [Academic Talk — Urban Geography] Why does the lecturer remark that the spillover explanation 'flatters the industries doing the explaining'?

options.A: To claim that researchers in this area are funded by the firms they study.
options.B: To show why patent citations are concentrated in a small number of places.
options.C: To offer a reason for the hypothesis's popularity that has nothing to do with how well it is evidenced.
options.D: To argue that technology firms understand agglomeration better than economists do.

51.stem: [Academic Talk — Origins of Writing] What is the professor’s main point about the development of writing systems?

options.A: Writing systems emerged independently in several regions, not from a single origin
options.B: The Maya script was shaped by Chinese writing carried east through early trade contact
options.C: Writing was first used only for religious purposes, as the Shang oracle bone records show
options.D: All writing systems can be traced back to the Mesopotamian cuneiform of about 3200 BCE

52.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] According to the professor, how does a glacier form?

options.A: In places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer, snow compresses into dense ice.
options.B: When ridges of debris called moraines trap meltwater that later refreezes into a thick sheet of ice.
options.C: When a river freezes solid through several unusually long winters and then creeps slowly downhill.
options.D: When gravity drags loose snow downhill until it collects in a U-shaped valley.

53.stem: [Academic Talk — Psychology] According to the professor, how can forgetting be beneficial?

options.A: It makes eyewitness memories more reliable as time passes.
options.B: It clears out outdated information so current information isn't buried.
options.C: It keeps the tip-of-the-tongue state from happening when you need a word fast.
options.D: It permanently strengthens the memories that are left after the rest fade.

54.stem: [Academic Talk — Film History] According to the professor, what did the Lumière brothers' films show?

options.A: Tricks discovered by accident when a camera jammed, making objects vanish.
options.B: Crowds of working-class and immigrant viewers filling the American nickelodeons.
options.C: Fantastical stories staged on painted sets, such as a rocket flying to the moon.
options.D: Ordinary scenes from everyday life, such as workers leaving a factory.

55.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] What tension does the professor point out about using interest rates to fight inflation?

options.A: Cutting rates fights inflation but slows economic growth
options.B: Raising rates lowers inflation but also makes borrowing cheaper
options.C: Raising rates only works if the central bank serves the public directly
options.D: The same tool that fights inflation can also cause unemployment

56.stem: [Academic Talk — History] What inference can be made about the speaker's view on the Industrial Revolution?

options.A: The speaker regards technological advancement as the only positive outcome.
options.B: The speaker thinks the Revolution was mainly detrimental to society.
options.C: The speaker believes the Revolution's costs outweighed its benefits.
options.D: The speaker sees the Revolution as a complex period with mixed outcomes.

57.stem: [Academic Talk — Epidemiology] Which result would the lecturer most likely accept as strengthening the case that coffee itself extends life?

options.A: A demonstration that coffee drinkers and non-drinkers in the cohort were matched on income, housing and occupation.
options.B: A cohort several times larger in which the very same association survives the very same adjustments by the same margin.
options.C: A steady rise in the benefit as consumption rises, of a shape no confounder is likely to reproduce.
options.D: A finding that the association disappears entirely once smoking is recorded in finer bands than simply yes or no.

58.stem: [Academic Talk — Institutional Economics] When the lecturer says the model 'quietly begs the question', he means that it

options.A: invites the audience to draw a moral conclusion the economics does not support.
options.B: builds in as an assumption the very thing it claims to have demonstrated.
options.C: demands more evidence from historians than the surviving records can supply.
options.D: raises an obvious further question that the parable itself leaves unanswered.

59.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] According to the speaker, what does the endowment effect describe?

options.A: People consistently pay far more for an item than a rational buyer would accept.
options.B: People would rather keep many inexpensive items than trade for a few valuable ones.
options.C: People rate things they already own above comparable things they do not own.
options.D: People rate scarce goods above goods that are widely available.

60.stem: [Academic Talk — Institutional Economics] What is the lecturer's attitude toward Hardin's parable of the pasture?

options.A: He holds that its central calculation is mistaken, since the private gain does not in fact exceed the shared cost.
options.B: He accepts it as a general law of resource use that the fieldwork has since confirmed in detail.
options.C: He treats its reasoning as sound but its reach as overstated, and keeps it for a narrow class of cases.
options.D: He rejects it outright, on the grounds that the fieldwork found no cheating or disputes among users.

61.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] What does the lecturer imply about measuring opportunity cost?

options.A: It is relevant only to societies allocating limited resources.
options.B: It is always a purely financial calculation.
options.C: It is usually ignored when individuals make everyday decisions.
options.D: It can be measured in terms other than money.

62.stem: [Academic Talk — Historiography] What is the lecturer's view of the older method of ranking sources by reliability?

options.A: He regards it as discredited, since documents written for a superior are systematically false.
options.B: He endorses it, provided the historian first determines which of the two writers was the more honest.
options.C: He shares its aim but faults it for assigning reliability to whole documents instead of to particular claims.
options.D: He objects that it ignores the purposes for which documents were written, which is the only thing now recoverable.

63.stem: [Academic Talk — History] What is the professor's main point about the Renaissance?

options.A: The Renaissance was a purely artistic movement, funded by Italian trade wealth but with no intellectual side.
options.B: The Renaissance rejected the ancient Greek and Roman texts that monasteries had spent centuries copying.
options.C: The Renaissance was a sudden rebirth of learning that broke with a medieval period that produced nothing.
options.D: The Renaissance is better understood as a gradual shift in outlook that built on medieval foundations.

64.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] Why does the professor mention the difference between U-shaped and V-shaped valleys?

options.A: To give hikers a way to tell that a glacier was once present.
options.B: To describe the way stacked snow is compressed into dense glacial ice.
options.C: To show that glaciers, being rivers of ice, flow faster than we assume.
options.D: To explain how retreating ice dumps its debris into ridges called moraines.

65.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] What is the professor's main point about behavioral economics?

options.A: That loss aversion and anchoring are the only biases that affect decisions
options.B: That people deviate from rational choice in systematic, predictable ways
options.C: That traditional economics has been proven completely correct by experiments
options.D: That people are fundamentally irrational and cannot be helped to decide well

66.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] Why does the professor introduce the idea of absolute advantage at the start of the talk?

options.A: To argue that absolute advantage and comparative advantage are the same thing
options.B: To set up a common intuition and then show it is not what actually drives trade
options.C: To explain how David Ricardo measured productivity in 1817
options.D: To prove that the country better at everything should never trade

67.stem: [Academic Talk — Asymmetric information in labor markets] What does the professor suggest about the use of educational credentials in hiring?

options.A: They are the only signal employers use when hiring for technical roles
options.B: They matter less and less because of credential inflation
options.C: They guarantee that a worker will be highly productive
options.D: They are an imperfect signal of a worker’s true ability

68.stem: [Academic Talk — Art History] What is the professor's main point about Gothic cathedrals?

options.A: A set of engineering innovations let builders raise tall, light-filled walls of stained glass that served both structure and faith.
options.B: Gothic builders kept the thick Romanesque walls and small windows, relying on the pointed arch alone for height.
options.C: The stained-glass windows were there for decoration only, since the congregation could read the biblical stories anyway.
options.D: Gothic cathedrals were admired above all for the strength of their round arches, which carried the roof's weight without any outside support.

69.stem: [Academic Talk — History of Technology] Why does the professor describe Eastman's slogan and the mailing of the camera back to the factory?

options.A: To explain how the negative-to-positive principle that finally won out was first discovered.
options.B: To describe how portraits had to be made in the years before the daguerreotype appeared.
options.C: To show how photography became something almost anyone could do, not just specialists.
options.D: To argue that the sharpness of the daguerreotype made it superior to Eastman's roll film.

70.stem: [Academic Talk — Disruptive Innovation] What is the main focus of the lecture?

options.A: The particular reasons Kodak's film business collapsed despite its own digital research
options.B: The importance of the medallion regulations that protected traditional taxi companies
options.C: How large established firms can prevent smaller rivals from entering their markets
options.D: The process by which new business models can transform industries

71.stem: [Academic Talk — Stellar nucleosynthesis] What does the professor clarify about the creation of elements heavier than iron?

options.A: They do not form naturally at all and appear only in laboratory experiments
options.B: They are formed during supernova explosions, not by fusion in stars
options.C: They are created in the Sun’s core by the proton-proton chain that fuses hydrogen
options.D: They are produced only in red giant stars, the source of much of the universe’s carbon

72.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] Why does the speaker bring up the endowment effect?

options.A: To define what economists mean when they call a decision rational.
options.B: To argue that behavioral economics has replaced traditional economic theory.
options.C: As evidence that consumers do not always behave the way the standard model predicts.
options.D: To show that ownership makes a good objectively more valuable than a similar good.

73.stem: [Academic Talk — Memory Distortion] What is the professor mainly emphasizing about memory?

options.A: That memory is dynamic and can be influenced by various factors
options.B: That memory stores a faithful record of what happened
options.C: That highly emotional events are remembered with the greatest accuracy
options.D: That people knowingly invent details they did not see

74.stem: [Academic Talk — Evolutionary Biology] What does the earthworm's kidney, taken together with the idea of ecological inheritance, imply about how a trait's persistence should be read?

options.A: That adaptation of a trait always lags some distance behind the environmental change that drives it.
options.B: That the soil environment must, over enough generations, have come to select for the very freshwater kidney that the worms have gone on retaining.
options.C: That a trait persisting in a habitat that does not suit it must be vestigial, and will be lost from the lineage once selection has had time enough to work.
options.D: That a lineage may answer a mismatch by altering its surroundings, so persistence is not proof the trait was shaped to fit those surroundings.

75.stem: [Academic Talk — Marine Biology] According to the professor, what do the algae provide to the coral?

options.A: Most of the food energy they make through photosynthesis.
options.B: The hard calcium carbonate skeleton that supports the reef.
options.C: The raw materials the polyp needs for its skeleton.
options.D: A sheltered place to live inside the polyp's tissues.

76.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] What does the professor mean by the tax base?

options.A: The lowest level of income at which a person first begins to pay any tax
options.B: The percentage rate that is charged on each dollar a person earns
options.C: The gap between a tax's stated rate and the real burden it imposes
options.D: What is being taxed, such as income, purchases, or property

77.stem: [Academic Talk — Zoology] Why does the professor emphasize the 'redundancy' of birds' navigation cues?

options.A: To show that young birds cannot migrate alone.
options.B: To argue that magnetism is the only reliable cue.
options.C: To prove that birds ignore the stars on cloudy nights.
options.D: To explain why migratory journeys so often succeed.

78.stem: [Academic Talk — Marine Biology] According to the professor, what causes coral bleaching?

options.A: When the water gets too warm, the stressed coral expels its algae and turns white.
options.B: When the polyps multiply faster than the calcium carbonate skeleton can support them.
options.C: When the algae multiply so quickly that they cover the polyps and block out the light.
options.D: When the coral lays down so much calcium carbonate that its skeleton hardens and whitens.

79.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] What is the primary purpose of the lecture?

options.A: To discuss only destructive plate boundaries.
options.B: To explain how plate tectonics shapes the Earth's surface and causes geological events.
options.C: To focus on the use of GPS in geology.
options.D: To describe the history of the Himalayas.

80.stem: [Academic Talk — Historiography] Why does the lecturer contrast a mob of two thousand with a scuffle of forty?

options.A: To settle how many people actually took part in the riot.
options.B: To show that a figure can be predicted from the writer's situation, so the discrepancy need not be settled by deciding who lied.
options.C: To suggest that large numbers in early documents were conventional rather than literal.
options.D: To show that official reports record quantities more precisely than private letters do.

81.stem: [Academic Talk - Earth Science] Given the evidence the talk sets out, which claim about the Cryogenian ocean is left standing, and in whose version?

options.A: That open water and a working water cycle ran through the glaciation, as Allen reads the Oman rock, with ice grinding bedrock near the equator all the same.
options.B: That the ocean froze over from pole to pole and stayed shut for millions of years, the carbon dioxide loading and the carbonate blanket at the top of each succession following from that closure.
options.C: That the diamictites are debris flows and storm beds of ordinary marine origin, the glaciation being a construction laid over rock that never called for one, which is Allen's position.
options.D: That equatorial ice calls for no global freeze at all, a tilt past fifty-four degrees making the tropics the coldest ground on the planet and putting glaciers there by geometry.

82.stem: [Academic Talk - Cell Biology] What is Martin's objection unable to settle?

options.A: Whether a cell that has no mitochondrion can maintain a genome any larger than the one a bacterium gets by with.
options.B: What the host was doing with the machinery it had, a claim about cost being silent on the use a structure is put to.
options.C: Whether the nucleus was in place before the mitochondrion or after it, which is a question of sequence, not of budget.
options.D: Whether the internal membranes of a mitochondrion are able to carry the machinery that reads genes off a chromosome.

83.stem: [Academic Talk — The Black Death] What does the professor imply about government attempts to control wages after the plague?

options.A: They encouraged more people to become farmhands
options.B: They were supported by the Church
options.C: They were effective in stabilizing the economy
options.D: They led to increased social unrest

84.stem: [Academic Talk — Communication] What is the main idea of the talk?

options.A: Social media is now the only form of communication that reaches a wide audience quickly.
options.B: Social media has now entirely replaced face-to-face conversation for most everyday purposes.
options.C: Face-to-face interaction is no longer necessary now that messages travel so fast and far.
options.D: Social media has changed communication but hasn't eliminated face-to-face interaction.

85.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] Why does the professor say 'nobody decides this price'?

options.A: To introduce the idea that governments must step in and set prices.
options.B: To emphasize that equilibrium arises from interaction rather than one party's choice.
options.C: To claim that prices move at random and cannot really be explained.
options.D: To argue that buyers ultimately have more power than sellers, since they can refuse to buy.

86.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] What can be inferred about the prediction of volcanic eruptions?

options.A: Only Hawaiian-style volcanoes can be monitored.
options.B: Prediction is impossible because eruptions give no signals.
options.C: Scientists can pinpoint the exact day an eruption will occur.
options.D: Monitoring gives useful warning even though the exact timing is uncertain.

87.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] What is the main idea of the talk?

options.A: Tectonic activity is the only force responsible for the Grand Canyon's formation.
options.B: The Grand Canyon was formed solely by the Colorado River.
options.C: The Grand Canyon's formation is due to multiple geological processes.
options.D: Erosion from wind and rain has had almost no effect on the canyon's present shape.

88.stem: [Academic Talk — Art / Perception] What is the professor's main point about color theory?

options.A: Only the three primary colors are perceived directly; the rest are inferred by the brain.
options.B: Color bears no reliable relation to wavelength, since one gray can look blue or warm.
options.C: Color is a perceptual construction shaped by context as much as by wavelength.
options.D: Color is a fixed physical property that objects possess on their own.

89.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] What can be inferred about the relationship between photosynthesis and respiration?

options.A: They are separate processes that never feed into each other.
options.B: Both processes give off oxygen as a waste product.
options.C: Respiration builds the sugar molecules that photosynthesis later breaks down.
options.D: Respiration releases the energy that photosynthesis stored in sugar.

90.stem: [Academic Talk — Meteorology] What is the professor's main point about how clouds form?

options.A: Clouds form when cool air sinks toward the ground, where it can hold less moisture.
options.B: Rain falls whenever a cloud forms, since the droplets in it are already heavy enough.
options.C: Clouds form when rising air cools and its water vapor condenses into droplets.
options.D: Clouds are simply masses of invisible water vapor that the wind has pushed upward.

91.stem: [Academic Talk - Astrophysics] Which position does the material presented leave standing?

options.A: That the ratio of mass to light assumed for a stellar disc is the source of the whole discrepancy, at every scale it appears.
options.B: That a halo of unseen matter, fitted galaxy by galaxy, accounts for the motions at every scale once the profile is corrected.
options.C: That the law relating force to motion departs from the familiar one wherever the pull is weak, which covers clusters as it covers spirals.
options.D: That something unseen is required where a galaxy is not the unit, while the regularity across spirals is not what halo histories yield.

92.stem: [Academic Talk — Renaissance perspective techniques] What is the main purpose of the lecture?

options.A: To describe how Filippo Brunelleschi worked out the rules of linear perspective in Florence
options.B: To argue that atmospheric perspective replaced linear perspective in later Renaissance work
options.C: To explain how Renaissance artists used perspective to create more realistic art
options.D: To compare Renaissance painting with the Roman murals that hinted at depth without rules

93.stem: [Academic Talk — Art History] What is the professor's main point about Impressionist painting?

options.A: The Impressionists painted mainly to record historical events as accurately as a document would.
options.B: The Impressionists reorganized their practice around capturing fleeting light rather than finishing in the studio.
options.C: The Impressionists were the first painters ever to take their work outdoors, since no one had sketched outside before.
options.D: The Impressionists gave up color for tonal drawing, since a blended surface demanded it.

94.stem: [Academic Talk — Linguistics] What does the asterisk before a Proto-Indo-European root indicate?

options.A: That the form is a reconstructed hypothesis with no surviving text.
options.B: That the word entered the language as a loan rather than by regular sound change.
options.C: That scholars have recovered a surviving written record of it.
options.D: That the word occurs more frequently than any other in the daughter languages.

95.stem: [Academic Talk — The Bystander Effect] What is the main idea of the lecture?

options.A: To trace the history of psychological research into emergencies from the 1960s onward.
options.B: To explain why people sometimes fail to help in emergencies when others are present.
options.C: To show that trained medical professionals are able to respond just as quickly in groups.
options.D: To argue that bystanders fail to act because they are fundamentally uncaring and apathetic.

96.stem: [Academic Talk — Geology] According to the professor, why does thick, sticky magma produce explosive eruptions?

options.A: Because thick magma carries no dissolved gas, so nothing can bubble out slowly.
options.B: Because it is low in silica and flows too quickly to cool.
options.C: Because it forms the slow rivers of lava seen in Hawaii.
options.D: Because gas gets trapped and pressure builds until it violently releases.

97.stem: [Academic Talk — Ecological Succession] Why does the professor say, "Actually — let me back up a moment"?

options.A: To concede that an abandoned field is not a true case of succession
options.B: To correct an earlier claim about which organisms colonise bare volcanic rock first
options.C: To add that secondary succession is not limited to abandoned farmland
options.D: To signal a shift toward the practical applications of succession research

98.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] What can be inferred about why a stock price might stay flat after good news?

options.A: Because the company chose not to pay out any dividends that quarter.
options.B: Because the news had already been expected and priced in.
options.C: Because shareholders cannot sell their shares quickly.
options.D: Because the company issued new shares that morning, diluting each one.

99.stem: [Academic Talk — Memory Distortion] Why does the professor mention the study involving groups watching a simulated crime?

options.A: To argue that group discussions improve memory accuracy
options.B: To demonstrate that only visual details are affected by distortion
options.C: To illustrate how social influence can alter individual memories
options.D: To show that people always remember crimes accurately

100.stem: [Academic Talk — Astronomy] According to the professor, why is there a tidal bulge on the far side of Earth?

options.A: Because the solid Earth is pulled away from that far water, leaving it behind.
options.B: Because the Sun's pull adds to the Moon's and stretches the far-side water outward.
options.C: Because the water there is closer to the Moon once the Earth has rotated at night.
options.D: Because steady winds push ocean water toward the side facing away from the Moon.

101.stem: [Academic Talk - Archaeology] Which narrowed version of the Cornish claim survives?

options.A: That tin travelled westward from central Asia throughout the second millennium, the Cornish workings serving a local market only.
options.B: That the isotope values identify Cornwall and Devon as the source of the metal in the two wrecks, the other regions being excluded by the trace metals.
options.C: That no ingot has an origin worth asking after, the metal in it having been melted and remixed too many times to carry a signature.
options.D: That the western deposits fed part of the later trade, without being where tin bronze began.

102.stem: [Academic Talk — History of Technology] What is the professor's main point about the early history of photography?

options.A: Photography was open to ordinary people from 1839 onward, long before roll film reached the market.
options.B: The daguerreotype stayed the standard because a single sharp plate could be reprinted whenever needed.
options.C: Photography advanced by solving the two problems of capturing an image and making copies of it.
options.D: Talbot's paper process was abandoned — because its softer images could never be printed more than once.

103.stem: [Academic Talk - Archaeology] The tablets from Mari occupy one sentence, unattached to what precedes or follows. What are they doing?

options.A: They confirm that tin was valuable enough to be priced against silver, which the palaces' consumption by the tonne had already implied.
options.B: They supply a dated written source against which the isotope ranges published for the second millennium can be calibrated and narrowed.
options.C: They put an eastern supply on record for a period earlier than the wrecks, which an unrestricted western account cannot hold.
options.D: They show the palaces supplied by their own kings rather than by traders, which alters who the wrecked cargoes belonged to when they sank.

104.stem: [Academic Talk — Evolutionary Biology] Why does the lecturer bring up beaver dams?

options.A: To supply a second, more familiar illustration of ecological inheritance than the earthworm.
options.B: Because it is the critics' example, offered to show that the older framework can redescribe such cases without difficulty.
options.C: To show that constructed environments commonly outlast the organisms that built them.
options.D: To argue that large-bodied animals reshape their habitats more thoroughly than small ones do.

105.stem: [Academic Talk — Economics] Why does the professor say students often miss the point that a monopolist is limited by the demand curve?

options.A: To suggest that the demand curve only constrains firms in perfectly competitive markets
options.B: To prove that monopolists always sell as much output as they possibly can
options.C: To argue that a monopolist ends up just as constrained as a wheat farmer who takes the price
options.D: To correct the misconception that a monopolist can set prices without any limit

106.stem: [Academic Talk — Origins of Writing] Why does the professor mention the gradual shift from pictorial to abstract forms in both Maya and Chinese scripts?

options.A: To show that pictorial signs recorded information better than abstract ones did
options.B: To illustrate a common developmental pattern in independent writing systems
options.C: To suggest that the Maya and Chinese scripts must have influenced one another
options.D: To argue that every writing system converges on the same set of abstract signs

107.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] Why does the professor mention identical twins?

options.A: To show that environment can shape outcomes even when DNA is identical.
options.B: To illustrate Mendel's dominant and recessive ratios.
options.C: To argue that twins always end up exactly the same height.
options.D: To prove that DNA has no effect on height.

108.stem: [Academic Talk — Astronomy] What can be inferred about spring tides from the lecture?

options.A: They happen when the Sun and the Moon stand at right angles to each other.
options.B: They are noticeably milder than the neap tides that come at right angles.
options.C: They occur only in the spring, which is how they got the name.
options.D: They occur at new and full moon when the Sun's and Moon's pulls combine.

109.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] Based on the talk, what would most likely follow a sharp decline in the sea otter population?

options.A: Urchins would starve because their main food source had disappeared.
options.B: The ecosystem would remain stable, since otters are not numerous to begin with.
options.C: Urchin numbers would rise and the kelp forest would be stripped away.
options.D: Kelp would grow more densely once a predator had been removed.

110.stem: [Academic Talk — Art History] Why does the professor mention that paint began to be sold in metal tubes?

options.A: To argue that studio painting was more expensive than outdoor work.
options.B: To show that the Impressionists invented a new kind of paint.
options.C: To explain what made painting outdoors in one session practical.
options.D: To explain why the Impressionists preferred darker colors.

111.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] What does the professor mean by saying 'genes load the dice'?

options.A: Genes matter only for simple traits; height is set entirely by childhood nutrition.
options.B: Genes shift the odds toward certain outcomes without deciding them alone.
options.C: The outcome is essentially random, since identical twins can end up at different heights.
options.D: Each trait is decided by a single dominant gene, exactly as in Mendel's pea plants.

112.stem: [Academic Talk — Linguistics] Why does the professor point out that no adult says 'goed'?

options.A: To argue that adults use forms like 'goed' around young children without realizing they do it.
options.B: To show that the child produced the form by applying a rule, not by imitation.
options.C: To explain that 'goed' is an acceptable past-tense form that adults have gradually stopped using.
options.D: To prove that the errors children make are copied from the adults they hear speaking every day.

113.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] What is the professor's main point about nitrogen?

options.A: Plants absorb nitrogen gas directly from the air, which is why the atmosphere is mostly nitrogen.
options.B: Nitrogen is abundant in the air but must be converted by bacteria before plants can use it.
options.C: Denitrifying bacteria are the most important part of the cycle, since they return nitrogen to the air.
options.D: Farmers invented crop rotation in order to add ammonia directly to the soil between plantings.

114.stem: [Academic Talk — Art History] According to the professor, which innovation was the key to letting the walls become thinner?

options.A: The thick supporting wall.
options.B: The round arch.
options.C: The stained-glass window.
options.D: The flying buttress.

115.stem: [Academic Talk — Psychology] Why does the professor mention an animal learning to press a lever for a treat?

options.A: To show that Pavlov also studied lever-pressing.
options.B: To contrast it as a different process from classical conditioning.
options.C: To give another example of classical conditioning.
options.D: To argue that treats work better than bells as signals.

116.stem: [Academic Talk - Palaeoecology] Given everything the lecturer sets out, which version of the hunting account is left standing?

options.A: That hunting mattered only on islands, where a small range and a small herd leave no room for recovery once a founding party lands.
options.B: That bands advancing at walking pace emptied each continent within a few centuries of setting foot on it, the front of that wave being what the staggering of the dates records.
options.C: That the reorganisation of the vegetation did the work, hunting adding a last increment to herds already confined to fragments too small to breed in.
options.D: That the losses follow the arrival of an unfamiliar predator, the timing tracking that arrival rather than the vegetation or the cold.

117.stem: [Academic Talk — Biology] What does the professor imply about farmers who rotated bean crops through their fields?

options.A: They rotated bean crops mainly to encourage the denitrifiers that return nitrogen gas to the air.
options.B: They were deliberately adding nitrogen gas to the soil, which plants can absorb straight from air.
options.C: They were benefiting from nitrogen fixation without understanding the chemistry behind it.
options.D: They already understood that the bacteria in the root nodules were converting N-two into ammonia.

118.stem: [Academic Talk — History of Technology] According to the professor, what was the serious limitation of the daguerreotype?

options.A: It could only be developed by sending the entire camera back to the factory.
options.B: It required a hundred-exposure roll of film loaded inside a simple box camera.
options.C: Each one was a unique object, with no negative to make additional prints.
options.D: Its images came out softer and less crisp than those of the rival paper process.

119.stem: [Academic Talk — Ecological Succession] The professor describes a New England forest study and then discusses human intervention. Taken together, what do these two points suggest?

options.A: Nurse plants are what let mosses and lichens colonize Mount St. Helens
options.B: The pace of succession is not fixed as local conditions and human action can change it
options.C: In wetter regions forests regrow on their own, so removing invasives makes no difference
options.D: Succession ends in a mature forest — whatever the climate or soil it starts from

120.stem: [Academic Talk — Architecture] What is the professor's main point about Roman architecture?

options.A: The Romans avoided the arch because it was structurally unreliable.
options.B: The Romans built mainly small private homes rather than public buildings.
options.C: The Romans copied Greek temples without changing anything.
options.D: The Romans' lasting achievement was engineering with concrete and the arch to enclose large public spaces.
